title: Why isn't "Simon Killer" (2012) a far more popular and critically-acclaimed film?

commenti.body: It's been a while since I have seen the film, I was very impressed with the story and characters. The filmmaker did a good job creating sympathy for Simon and then slowly reveal who he really is. It also felt like a neo-noir to me.

Yeah, that's another thing I really loved about it. Like not only is he manipulating the women in this film. He's also manipulating us. And when the true colors are revealed, that's when the characters also come to realize what he is. Even the first scenes where he is shown in isolation gives us this idea that he is someone who has some emotional problems and desperation that he needs to resolve. The masturbation scene shows that perfectly in a very uncomfortable way. It makes you believe he's just a guy that just needs someone. And in a way, he is but he also sabotages those relationships through his destructive behavior.

Yeah it's a real sleeper. From the little I understand, the Borderline Films boys made it very cheaply, so even though it looks pretty glossy I don't think they had much money behind it. I remember Antonio Campos talking about how they blagged their way in to the Louvre, to shoot the opening scene. And it falls in an awkward middle between genre and arthouse, American and European, which I think makes for a great mix, but I expect it was hard for distributors to sell it towards a certain audience/taste.

It was probably also ahead of its time - a few years pre-MeToo - those conversations about masculine entitlement / incel-ish behaviour weren't as central in the culture in 2012. I'd be interested to watch it again to see how differently it resonates now.

Pretty hardcore cast alumni - you probably know that Brady Corbett has just directed THE BRUTALIST, and Mati Diop, the other lead actor, has directed a few arthouse hits like ATLANTICS and DAHOMEY.

Quite a fascinating artefact for anyone who's a fan of those movies...

Can't help cuz I haven't seen it, but wanted to thank you for the post because I see this is the director who made Christine right after and that film definitely hit with me. Plus I see he's created a couple shows I really liked. So I'll be putting this one at the time of my watch list.

> Why isn't "Simon Killer" (2012) a far more popular 

It came out before streaming was really that common, it was released into only five theaters, nobody saw it. Most people have never heard of it. I follow most movies (as many as I can) and I'd never heard of it (that I can remember—I may have known about it since I was at Sundance that year). But really it's just because, like most films, nobody ever saw it.'

Compare to the 200th most-popular movie that year, "The East" that was in 195 theaters. 

It's really, really hard to get eyes on any particular movie. It's not that it's slow or fast or makes people unconfortable, it's that it never made it in front of people.

I caught this when it first came out and I’ve thought about it many times over the years. The Spectral Display song “It takes a muscle to fall in love” has been a regular in my musical rotation ever since.  I will rewatch tonight!

It was made by a director who isn't a mainstream name, stars an actor who has mostly starred in smaller indie films and is now an arthouse director, it didn't have a wide release, and nobody from it has gone onto to become a household name so it hasn't had a revival. It's also not a very easy film to love - the main character is unpleasant, it's filmed in a very stark, cold way, and the whole experience is quite a difficult one.

It's a great film. Weirdly, it was the most influential film to me when I was a film student. I basically wanted to copy the filming style and use of sound in every short film I made. There's a bit I particular love where he puts in headphones and provides the soundtrack while he follows someone, which I always thought was a neat touch.

Also, the soundtrack is fantastic. I discovered two of my favourite songs from it.

I actually watched this last night . I quite liked the overall atmosphere and tone, and the character exploration of Simon, to an extent. He is one toxic motherfucker and it was interesting to see this portrayed in a grounded manner. Simon is as much a victim of himself, in addition to those around him. But ultimately i thought it went a bit nowhere. There was no real pay off to justify the slow pacing, or no real point being made, story-wise, or even thematically. We watch Simon being toxic for an hour and fourty minutes, and then that's it. I don't mind open-ended films, but this was a little bit on the repetitive side. 5/10

I disagree personally. The point of seeing the repetition of his actions is exactly the point of the film. It is further emphasizing the pattern of behavior he is working around with his victims and showing the slow process of how he gaslights and manipulates to his desires. It's very intoxicating to watch and it makes you part of the obnoxious side effects of his actions. It's terrible to watch and Simon will never be truly change as a person nor find any true healthy relationships in his path because he's doomed to his narcissistic tendencies. It's nihilistic and pointless because that's just what it is. I think it works ver effectively for what it is going for and I don't think the way it portrays this type of abuse hasn't been replicated as accurately and uncomfortable as many other films that try to find it more excitment and sensationalism to something pathetic and repugnant.

I do agree with your general points, and how it was an almost unique take on a toxic character. But as i said, i found myself wanting a little more meat towards the end, whatever that could have been. By the time he meets the other french girl again (and what are the chances of that happening in Paris, but whatever, it's a minor point), we had a pretty good take on who Simon was. But here we were, watching the same thing again. I would have prefered if the film had continued to build on the story that we had been watching all along with Victoria. Yes, it shows us that Simon will always destroy every relationship he is in because that's who he is, but i did not find that as engaging as i would have liked. 

Anyway, i'm glad you liked it. Cheers.
